newsitem.title: UK: Battle to break up UK's Co-op to intensify - paper.
newsitem.headline: Battle to break up UK's Co-op to intensify - paper.

text.p: Attempts to break-up Britain's Co-operative Wholesale Society (CWS) are expected to intensify with the entrepreneur behind the move backing calls for a special general meeting to covert it into a company and then sell him some of its businesses, the Sunday Telegraph reported.

The paper said entrepreneur Andrew Regan is planning to ask 10 corporate members of the CWS to call a special general meeting at the end of May and is expected to begin his campaign later this week. The CWS has said it has no intention of selling its businesses.
CWS has interests ranging from supermarkets and farms to funeral parlours and travel agencies. It also owns a bank and an insurance company, both reported to be targeted by Regan.

The Sunday Telegraph said Regan, whose Lanica Trust made an approach to the CWS in February to discuss buying some of the CWS non-food businesses, was still finalising plans. But the special meeting wouild it said consider two motions, including coverting the CWS to a limited company.

The second would be to sell its non-food businesses, to Galileo, a vehicle set up by Regan for the bid. This plan would give CWS members "not only a share of the 500 million pounds ($813.8 million) that Regan is offering to pay for the non-food businesses but also some residual equity", it said.
CWS corporate members who hold about 40 percent of the vote in the society would, it said, share in a 200 million pound bonanza while its 500,000 private members would take about 600 pounds each.

The Sunday Telegraph said the CWS results, due to be published on Monday, were expected to be poor. Pre-tax profits are expected to fall to 14.0 million pounds for 1996 from 31.4 million pounds the year before on sales of more than 3.0 billion pounds.

The Sunday Times, which reported the same figures and said they had come from draft accounts, said trading profits fell to 48.8 million pounds from 48.8 million pounds and the CWS took a 5.6 million pounds on pulling out of peripheral activities.
Earlier this month the Co-operative Bank, which is owned by the CWS, announced pre-tax profits of 45.5 million pounds for the year to January 11, 1997.
